difficulty.rationale: Standard AP Physics 1 flat-curve friction item. Part A asks for a qualitative proportional-reasoning argument: required friction is proportional to v^2, so doubling speed quadruples it, and the claim is rejected. Part B has the student set f_s,max = mu_s*m*g equal to m*v^2/r, derive v = sqrt(mu_s*g*r), and compute about 15.7 m/s. Part C asks whether mass cancels, so max speed stays the same. All three parts use one governing model (Newton's second law with centripetal acceleration and static friction). The arithmetic is a single square root, the reading load is short, the wording is unambiguous, and everything is within Unit 2 scope. Difficulty comes from choosing the law and from the proportional and cancellation reasoning, not from unfair sources.

answers.brief_reasoning: Static friction is the only horizontal force, so it supplies the centripetal force: f = mv²/r. Since f depends on v², doubling the speed makes the needed friction four times as large, not twice.
answers.final_answer: Disagree: the friction needed goes up by a factor of 4, because f = mv²/r is proportional to v².

answers.brief_reasoning: The largest friction available is μs·mg. Setting μs·mg = m·v²/r gives v_max = sqrt(μs·g·r) = sqrt(0.6 × 9.8 × 60) ≈ 18.8 m/s.
answers.final_answer: v_max = sqrt(μs g r) ≈ 18.8 m/s (≈19 m/s; using g = 10 m/s² gives ≈19.0 m/s)

answers.brief_reasoning: Doubling the mass doubles both the maximum friction (μs·mg) and the force needed (mv²/r). The mass cancels, so v_max = sqrt(μs·g·r) does not change.
answers.final_answer: Stays the same
